title: “Ye waters that be above the heavens” — which waters does Psalm 148:4 call on to praise?
summary: Psalm 148:4 calls on “ye heavens of heavens, and ye waters that be above the heavens” to praise the Lord. The verses quoted do not say which waters these are, where they are, or whether they are the waters that Genesis 1:7 places above the firmament.
text: KJV Psalms 148:3–4: “Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light.” “Praise him, ye heavens of heavens, and ye waters that be above the heavens.” KJV Psalms 148:5–6: “Let them praise the name of the Lord: for he commanded, and they were created.” “He hath also stablished them for ever and ever: he hath made a decree which shall not pass.” KJV Genesis 1:6–8: “And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.” “And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament: and it was so.” “And God called the firmament Heaven. And the evening and the morning were the second day.”
reasoning: Psalm 148:4 names two things after “Praise him”: “ye heavens of heavens” and “ye waters that be above the heavens”. Psalm 148:5–6 say of “them” that they were created at the Lord’s command and established for ever by a decree. The verses quoted do not say which waters are above the heavens, where the heavens are, or what separates the two. Genesis 1:7 speaks of “the waters which were above the firmament” and Genesis 1:8 calls the firmament “Heaven”, so a reader may take the psalm to speak of the same waters. Possible readings: (1) the waters of Genesis 1:6–7, with the “heavens” of the psalm as the firmament Genesis 1:8 calls Heaven; (2) waters the psalm names without reference to Genesis; (3) a call to praise that names a part of creation without saying what it is. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted. The record does not examine other passages about waters above the heavens, does not say that any reading is the right one, and does not set the psalm against Genesis or against any account of the sky. The published records on the Genesis firmament are separate and are not examined here.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: ye waters that be above the heavens

title: “The judgment written” — which writing does Psalm 149:9 mean?
summary: Psalm 149:9 speaks of executing “the judgment written” upon those named in 149:7–8. The verses quoted do not say where it is written, by whom, or what the judgment is.
text: KJV Psalms 149:6–7: “Let the high praises of God be in their mouth, and a two-edged sword in their hand;” “To execute vengeance upon the heathen, and punishments upon the people;” KJV Psalms 149:8–9: “To bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with fetters of iron;” “To execute upon them the judgment written: this honour have all his saints. Praise ye the Lord.” A search of the packaged KJV for the words “judgment written” finds Psalms 149:9 only.
reasoning: Psalm 149:7–9 list acts that are to be done by those who have “the high praises of God … in their mouth, and a two-edged sword in their hand”: vengeance on the heathen, punishments on the people, binding their kings and nobles, and executing “the judgment written”. The last item is the only one that refers to something written. The verses quoted do not name a book or a place where the judgment is written, do not say who wrote it, and do not say what it contains. Possible readings: a judgment recorded in a writing the psalm does not name; a judgment already pronounced in a text the reader is assumed to know; or a phrase used for a judgment that is certain. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted; the word search covers the packaged KJV text only and is a word search. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, and does not examine other passages about vengeance or judgment.

title: “From the hand of strange children” — who are the strange children of Psalm 144:7 and 144:11?
summary: Psalm 144:7 and 144:11 ask for rescue “from the hand of strange children”, whose “mouth speaketh vanity” and whose right hand is “a right hand of falsehood”. The verses quoted do not say whose children they are or what makes them strange.
text: KJV Psalms 144:7–8: “Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children;” “Whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.” KJV Psalms 144:11: “Rid me, and deliver me from the hand of strange children, whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood:” KJV Hosea 5:7: “They have dealt treacherously against the Lord: for they have begotten strange children: now shall a month devour them with their portions.” A search of the packaged KJV for the words “strange children” finds Psalms 144:7, Psalms 144:11 and Hosea 5:7 only.
reasoning: The psalm asks twice to be delivered from the hand of “strange children”, and describes them by their speech (“vanity”) and by their right hand (“a right hand of falsehood”). The verses quoted do not say whose children they are, from where, or whether “strange” marks them as foreign or as estranged in some other sense. In Hosea 5:7 the same two English words occur in a sentence about people who “have dealt treacherously against the Lord” and “have begotten strange children”; the record quotes it as context and does not say that the psalm means the same group or the same sense. Possible readings: foreigners who are enemies of the speaker’s people; persons of the speaker’s own people who act as foreigners; or a phrase used in the psalm in a sense the verses quoted do not define. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted; the word search covers the packaged KJV text only and is a word search. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, and does not examine the other verses of Psalm 144 or the parallel material in other psalms.
